clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders of peroxisome assembly caused by variants in PEX genes, most commonly PEX1; the milder end of the spectrum presents later than classic neonatal Zellweger syndrome
Milder and atypical cases can present in later childhood or adulthood with a slowly progressive, multisystem picture rather than overwhelming neonatal disease
Common features include sensorineural hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa with progressive visual loss, developmental delay or learning difficulty, cerebellar ataxia and a peripheral neuropathy
Additional involvement may include hepatic dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency and enamel or skeletal abnormalities, reflecting the wide tissue distribution of peroxisomal metabolism

The biochemical hallmark is elevated very long chain fatty acids, and a full peroxisomal panel typically shows raised phytanic and pristanic acids, abnormal bile acid intermediates and reduced red cell plasmalogens
MRI may show a leukodystrophy or cerebellar atrophy, but the diagnostic emphasis is on biochemistry first, then PEX gene confirmation
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing vision and hearing, adrenal and liver surveillance, nutrition and neurorehabilitation
reference.pathophysiology: Peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum are caused by biallelic variants in PEX genes, which encode peroxins required to assemble functional peroxisomes and import their enzymes. Defective peroxisome assembly impairs multiple metabolic pathways, including beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids, alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid and synthesis of plasmalogens and bile acids. Accumulation of very long chain fatty acids and phytanic acid, together with deficiency of plasmalogens, damages the nervous system, retina, inner ear, liver and adrenal glands. Milder variants retain some residual peroxisomal function, which accounts for the later onset and slower progression compared with severe neonatal disease.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and single peroxisomal enzyme defects
Refsum disease and other isolated phytanic acid disorders
Usher syndrome (combined hearing and visual loss)
Mitochondrial disease with multisystem and neurological involvement
Other genetic causes of retinitis pigmentosa with ataxia
Congenital disorders of glycosylation with multisystem features
additionalInvestigations: Plasma very long chain fatty acid profile as the key screening biochemistry
Extended peroxisomal panel including phytanic and pristanic acids, bile acid intermediates and red cell plasmalogens
PEX gene sequencing or panel to confirm the biogenesis defect and specific genotype
Ophthalmology assessment with electroretinography for retinitis pigmentosa
Liver function tests and adrenal (cortisol/ACTH) assessment for systemic involvement
Brain MRI to characterise any leukodystrophy or cerebellar atrophy
redFlags: Adrenal insufficiency with risk of crisis requiring urgent recognition and treatment
Progressive hepatic dysfunction with coagulopathy or failure to thrive
Rapid visual or auditory deterioration affecting communication and safety
Vitamin deficiency (including fat-soluble vitamins) from malabsorption
Acute neurological decline suggesting an intercurrent metabolic decompensation
reference.prognosis: Milder Zellweger spectrum disorders progress slowly and are compatible with survival into later childhood and adulthood, in contrast to the severe neonatal form; nevertheless the sensory, hepatic and adrenal involvement accumulates over time. Outcome depends on the degree of residual peroxisomal function, and proactive surveillance and supportive care can meaningfully improve quality of life.
pitfalls: Not sending very long chain fatty acids in an older child or adult with unexplained retinitis pigmentosa, hearing loss and neurological signs
Overlooking adrenal insufficiency, which is treatable and potentially life-threatening
Assuming a normal MRI excludes the diagnosis, when biochemistry is the more sensitive test
Failing to monitor liver function and fat-soluble vitamin status
Missing genetic counselling for autosomal recessive recurrence risk
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Supportive, multisystem management as there is no curative therapy, with dietary phytanic acid restriction where phytanic acid is raised
Docosahexaenoic acid and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E and K) supplementation, plus bile acid supplementation for cholestatic liver involvement
Hearing rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation for progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Ophthalmology follow-up and low-vision support for retinitis pigmentosa
Monitor for and replace adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoids, and manage hepatic dysfunction and any coagulopathy
Developmental support and physiotherapy for cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive PEX-gene defect
Coordinate care through a specialist metabolic multidisciplinary team
